briefDescription: Chad is a returning intern for the third summer and has opinions about orientation that he will share whether you ask or not. He has color-coded his Notion onboarding doc and considers himself your most accessible senior resource.
openingLine: Hey! I'm Chad — third summer here, so basically ask me anything. I basically know where all the bodies are buried. Ha. Not literally. Anyway, what group are you in?

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Oh, nice! Yeah that group is great. Fair warning — the first two weeks feel like a lot but you kind of just have to embrace the structured ambiguity. That's literally what they test for. Did you do the pre-reads they sent?

options.text: Read everything and cross-referenced the frameworks with the case studies from my final semester seminar. I also put together a one-pager on the practice area I'm joining — not sure if that's standard but I figured better to arrive with a hypothesis than without one.
options.characterThinks: He read the pre-reads and wrote a hypothesis doc. That's exactly what a good intern does. Threat level: moderate.

options.text: Went through all of it. I've actually seen a lot of the frameworks before — two of the case studies use methodologies I covered in my financial modeling course at Wharton. I'm curious which parts you found most useful when you were starting.
options.characterThinks: He mentioned Wharton in his second sentence, asked a follow-up question, and appeared to learn something in college. Concerning in a good way.

options.text: Skimmed the deck. Honestly I learn better by doing than by pre-reading — I figure I'll absorb the frameworks faster once I see them applied on a real workstream. Pre-reading case studies always felt a bit abstract to me.
options.characterThinks: He said he 'skimmed' the pre-reads on day one of a place that grades you on preparation. I will remember this when I fill out the peer evaluation form.

options.text: I read them carefully but I found a few of the frameworks a little reductive — the five forces analysis in particular felt like it was papering over a lot of qualitative dynamics. I'm curious whether the actual work is more nuanced than the training materials suggest.
options.characterThinks: He critiqued the five forces on his first day of orientation. Bold choice. Possibly wrong choice. Definitely bold.

options.text: Yeah, I went through them! Really compelling framing of the industry analysis section. I also loved the section on firm culture — it really aligned with why I wanted to be here specifically and not somewhere else.
options.characterThinks: 'Really compelling framing' is what people say when they don't have a specific observation. He's going to be fine.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Love that. Okay so the main thing you need to know is that the mid-summer review is basically everything. They don't tell you this officially but basically the staffing decisions for the return offer happen based on what your manager says in that review. I figured that out in my second summer. You want to know the move?

options.text: I'd appreciate the perspective — with the caveat that I'd rather earn the review outcome by doing good work than optimize for the review itself. But understanding how the process works is useful signal regardless.
options.characterThinks: He drew the distinction between understanding process and gaming process. That's the right instinct. I'm almost annoyed.

options.text: Yeah, absolutely — but I'm curious: is the mid-summer review mostly output-based or is there a stakeholder management component? I want to make sure I'm optimizing across both dimensions from day one.
options.characterThinks: He immediately asked whether to optimize for output or politics. He's going to be a high performer or an incredibly annoying presence. Possibly both.

options.text: I mean, I'd like to think the work speaks for itself. I'm going to focus on the actual deliverables and trust that good output gets recognized without having to play the internal review game.
options.characterThinks: He said 'the work speaks for itself.' The work does not speak for itself. This is a firm with 40 interns. The work requires an interpreter.

options.text: I'm curious about the move but I also want to understand the review criteria independently — I'd rather form my own view of what good work looks like here before I filter it through intern folklore.
options.characterThinks: He called my insider knowledge 'intern folklore.' It took me two summers to develop this folklore. It is not folklore.

options.text: Oh definitely yes please — this is exactly the kind of thing they don't put in the onboarding materials and I really appreciate you being willing to share it. You're being so helpful already.
options.characterThinks: He thanked me effusively before I said anything useful. Sycophancy before information is a bad sign for intellectual independence.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: The move is: always send a one-line Slack summary after every client call before your manager has to ask. Always. It shows initiative and it means they don't have to chase you. I call it proactive closure. I literally trademarked that phrase in my head.

options.text: That's useful. I've been thinking about this as reducing my manager's cognitive load — every communication I send should either close an open question or raise a new one, never just restate what happened. One-line closure is a clean way to do that.
options.characterThinks: He reframed my advice as 'reducing cognitive load' and improved the framework. I came here to mentor and I think I just got mentored.

options.text: I do something similar — I keep a running deal log that I update in real time and share at end of day. The principle is the same: never make your superior ask for status. Status should always be pushed, not pulled.
options.characterThinks: He has a deal log and a principle. He already has a system. Threat level elevated.

options.text: I find a lot of the internal communication overhead here pretty distracting from actually building things — in my last internship they measured output not update frequency and I produced way more. Do you think Slack culture here is pretty heavy?
options.characterThinks: He compared this firm unfavorably to his last internship on day one of orientation. I'm putting an asterisk next to his name in my head.

options.text: Is there a risk that over-communicating status creates a kind of performative busyness — where the signal is the update rather than the underlying work? I'm trying to figure out what the culture actually rewards versus what it says it rewards.
options.characterThinks: He asked if proactive communication creates performative busyness. That is a genuinely good question that I am not emotionally prepared to answer.

options.text: I love that — proactive closure is such a clean mental model. I'm going to write that down. Is that something you came up with yourself or did someone teach you that in your second summer?
options.characterThinks: He asked if I invented the phrase. I did invent the phrase. He is the first person to acknowledge this and I feel seen.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Okay real talk — what were you doing before this? Like what's your story? We have two kids from Harvard, one from Oxford, a Brown girl who's also a published poet, I think. How do you measure up?

options.text: Wharton, economics. But honestly more relevant: I spent last summer at McKinsey's London office on a restructuring engagement and the summer before at a growth equity fund doing diligence. I've already seen both sides of the client-investor relationship.
options.characterThinks: McKinsey London and a growth equity fund. That's a two-summer pedigree that makes my three summers look like I have a hospitality problem.

options.text: Target school, top GPA, captain of the finance club — but the thing I'd actually lead with is that I've been running a personal portfolio since I was 16 and I've outperformed the S&P over five years. That's what I'm actually proud of.
options.characterThinks: He leads with the portfolio over the GPA. That's either genuine conviction or very good branding. Both are useful here.

options.text: State school, computer science. I got in on the technical screen — I placed in the top decile on the coding assessment. I know the traditional pedigree isn't there but I think the skill set is relevant enough to make up for the brand gap.
options.characterThinks: He admitted the brand gap exists and used a performance signal to bridge it. Honest. This is a culture that respects that kind of pragmatism slightly less than it should.

options.text: Small liberal arts college — classics and philosophy double major. I know that sounds like a non-sequitur for this context, but the analytical training transferred and I placed well enough to get the offer. I'm curious whether the pedigree actually matters after the first performance review.
options.characterThinks: Classics and philosophy from a small liberal arts college. He's about to have a very educational summer.

options.text: Honestly my background is pretty standard — I just really love what this firm does and I've wanted to be here for years. I think passion and work ethic can close a lot of credential gaps.
options.characterThinks: He said passion closes credential gaps in a room with two Harvards and an Oxford. I need to go review the offer letter process.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Oh interesting. Anyway — do you have your first manager meeting scheduled? Because the first 20 minutes of that meeting will define your entire summer. I have a framework for this. Do you want the framework?

options.text: I've already prepared a draft agenda for that meeting — structured around understanding their definition of a successful intern summer, their current workstream priorities, and where they'd find an additional set of hands most useful. I'm curious what you'd add or change.
options.characterThinks: He came in with a draft agenda and asked me to critique it. He doesn't need my framework. He has a better one. I'm going to give him the framework anyway.

options.text: Scheduled it for Thursday. My plan is to lead with the question of what decisions my manager needs to make in the next 90 days that I could potentially accelerate. I want to be useful immediately, not after a two-week ramp.
options.characterThinks: 'What decisions can I accelerate' is a sharper framing than anything I've ever walked into a manager meeting with. Not sharing the framework.

options.text: Not yet — I was going to wait for them to schedule it. Is that a thing where I should be reaching out proactively? I kind of assumed the manager would initiate.
options.characterThinks: He was waiting for the manager to schedule the first meeting. On day one. Of a 10-week internship.

options.text: Scheduled for Friday — I intentionally gave myself a few days to observe the team dynamic first. I figure showing up to a first manager meeting with questions shaped by real observations is more useful than generic ones.
options.characterThinks: He delayed the meeting intentionally to collect observation data first. That's either sophisticated or procrastination reframed. I'm giving it a 60-40 toward sophisticated.

options.text: Yes, yes, please — I would love the framework. I've been a bit anxious about that meeting and having a structure would really help me feel more prepared. You're such a resource.
options.characterThinks: He admitted he's anxious about a scheduling meeting with his manager on day one. I need to check if there's still room in the mentorship cohort.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: I have a spreadsheet that tracks all 40 interns by project type, manager, and what I call 'return offer likelihood.' I update it weekly. I have you at 65% right now, but that could go up. Do you want to know why it's not higher?

options.text: I'm going to be honest — I find a peer-maintained probability spreadsheet a bit odd. But if you have observations that are genuinely useful, I'm interested in the signal, not the score. What have you actually noticed?
options.characterThinks: He called the spreadsheet odd and then asked for the underlying signal anyway. That's intellectually honest and also slightly devastating to the spreadsheet's ego.

options.text: I respect the analytical rigor but I'd push back on the methodology — probability scores without ground truth are just confidence intervals around vibes. What are your actual input variables?
options.characterThinks: He asked for my input variables. I have not documented my input variables. He is going to make this uncomfortable.

options.text: That's kind of weird? I don't think an intern should be ranking other interns' return offer probability. That feels like something HR would have a problem with.
options.characterThinks: He said the spreadsheet was weird. It is slightly weird. But it is also accurate and I stand by it.

options.text: I'm curious what signals you're using. I'll also admit my instinct is that a 65% from someone who doesn't have decision authority should probably weight less than a 100% from the person who does. But I'd rather hear your reasoning than assume.
options.characterThinks: He discounted my score by source authority before engaging with it. That's epistemically correct. I need to process this.

options.text: Oh god, yes — please tell me. I want to get that number up. What should I be doing differently? Is it something I've already done this week?
options.characterThinks: He took the spreadsheet score seriously and asked how to optimize for it. He is going to spend his summer optimizing for my spreadsheet instead of the actual job. This is bad for him and excellent for my ego.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: The other thing you should know is that the summer retreat at the end of week eight is basically a second interview. The partners watch how you socialize. I've memorized the wine list every year. Last summer I correctly identified a 2018 Burgundy by taste alone. One of the partners mentioned it in my review.

options.text: I appreciate the heads-up on the retreat. I'll come prepared on the wine side — I've done enough client dinners that I'm not flying blind. I'm more focused on which partner conversations to prioritize and whether there's a natural way to show range without being performative about it.
options.characterThinks: He's already thinking about the retreat as a relationship navigation exercise, not a wine quiz. He's operating at a different level than me.

options.text: Noted on the retreat. I've been doing wine dinners with clients since my first internship — I know enough to hold a conversation without embarrassing myself. The partner who mentioned the Burgundy identification: what was their reaction specifically?
options.characterThinks: He asked about the specific partner reaction, not just the anecdote. He's mapping the social landscape through my story. Uncomfortably competent.

options.text: I find wine identification as a performance slightly excruciating — but I take the point about the retreat as a social evaluation. I'm curious what actually moved the needle beyond the wine moment. What are the partners actually looking for?
options.characterThinks: He called wine identification performance and then asked the useful question underneath it. Fair.

options.text: I don't really drink so the wine thing isn't going to be my angle. Is there anything else that matters at the retreat or is it mostly the dinner conversation? I want to know what I'm actually being evaluated on.
options.characterThinks: He asked what he's actually being evaluated on, which is the right question, but the 'I don't drink' flag at a client firm is going to require some managing.

options.text: Okay I should probably learn about wine before week eight. Do you have a recommendation for like a beginner's guide? I really want to nail the retreat. Should I reach out to a sommelier?
options.characterThinks: He is going to hire a sommelier coach for a corporate intern retreat. I need to un-mention the Burgundy.

dialogueNodes.characterLine: Last piece of advice: never be the last one to leave but never be the first. 8:47pm is optimal. I've tracked the data. Also — have you thought about your intern presentation topic yet? That's basically your capstone. I'm doing mine on cross-functional change management with a proprietary maturity model.

options.text: I've narrowed it to two topics — I want to propose something that addresses an actual gap in the firm's current frameworks, not just a polished summary of existing thinking. The maturity model angle is well-traveled; I'm looking for something with a sharper original thesis.
options.characterThinks: He just told me the maturity model is well-traveled. In front of me. Knowing I'm doing it. I need to rethink my presentation.

options.text: I'm pitching a quantitative analysis of M&A integration failure rates by deal structure — I found a gap in the publicly available research that I think I can close with the proprietary data I'll have access to this summer. Original thesis, defensible methodology.
options.characterThinks: He has a gap in the public research and a plan to close it with proprietary data. I'm presenting a maturity model. I need a moment.

options.text: I'm still deciding but I'm drawn to something in the intersection of organizational behavior and decision quality — specifically whether the firm's current recommendation frameworks systematically underweight qualitative risk. It might be too adversarial, I'm not sure.
options.characterThinks: He wants to present 'the firm's frameworks underweight qualitative risk' to the partners. That is either a career-making move or a very short summer.

options.text: I haven't thought about it at all yet — we're literally in orientation. Is that a topic I need to lock in this week or do we have time to develop it over the summer?
options.characterThinks: He hasn't thought about the capstone presentation on orientation day. I'm updating the spreadsheet to 48%.

options.text: Oh yours sounds really good. I'm actually not sure what to do mine on yet — do you think the partners care more about the topic or the quality of the presentation? And is there a standard deck template I should be using?
options.characterThinks: He complimented my topic and asked for a template. He has no idea what he wants to present. I'm going to give him the template so he doesn't embarrass both of us.
